detail:
Mayo Clinic explains that migraine is diagnosed by a doctor trained in headaches, usually a neurologist, from the medical history, the symptoms, and a physical and neurological examination; there is no specific test for it. Frequency draws the line between the two main patterns: episodic migraine means headache on fewer than 15 days a month, while chronic migraine means headache on 15 or more days a month for more than three consecutive months.

Research described by Mayo suggests migraine involves changes in neurotransmitters and neuropeptides in the brain, including calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), which several newer treatments target. Imaging such as MRI or CT is used when a headache pattern is unusual, complex, or suddenly severe, to rule out other causes rather than to confirm migraine.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about any new, changed, or suddenly severe headache pattern.

summary: Mayo Clinic distinguishes chronic migraine from episodic migraine by frequency: headache on 15 or more days per month for more than three months. Diagnosis is based on medical history, symptoms, and a physical and neurological examination rather than a single test.
takeaways: chronic migraine is counted in headache days per month
diagnosis rests on history and a neurological exam
scans are used to rule out other causes when patterns are unusual
a headache diary helps your doctor classify your pattern
title: Chronic migraine: headache on 15 or more days a month
